html:
From 1928 Soviet policy forced the nomadic Kazakhs to give up their herds and settle on collective farms. It ended a pastoral way of life that had lasted for thousands of years and caused one of the worst famines of the century.

It started in 1928 with the seizure of the herds of wealthy Kazakh families. Under the party chief Filipp Goloshchyokin, and as part of Stalin's drive for collectivisation, officials then took most of the livestock of ordinary herders and ordered them into fixed settlements. Little had been prepared: there were few houses, little fodder and no tools for farming. The animals died in huge numbers, and grain quotas took what food was left.

The result was the Kazakh famine of 1930 to 1933, in which between 1.3 and 2.3 million people died, close to 40 percent of all Kazakhs. Many others fled to China, Mongolia and the other Soviet republics. Kazakhs became a minority in their own land for decades.
sum: From 1928 Soviet policy forced the nomadic Kazakhs to give up their herds and settle on collective farms. It ended a pastoral way of life that had lasted for thousands of years and caused one of the worst famines of the century.
